ceb.title: The Anointing of the Sick
ceb.question: What is the Anointing of the Sick? Is it just 'Last Rites' for people who are dying?
ceb.answer: The Anointing of the Sick is a sacrament of healing given to those who are seriously ill or facing the frailty of old age, not merely a ritual for the dying. Its direct biblical mandate is found in James, who instructs the sick to call the presbyters (priests) of the Church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the name of the Lord, promising that the prayer of faith will save the sick person, the Lord will raise them up, and their sins will be forgiven (Jas 5:14-15). Jesus' own apostles anointed the sick with oil and healed them (Mk 6:13). The sacrament confers grace, spiritual strength, peace, courage, union with Christ's passion, and forgiveness of sins, and when God wills, physical healing. It can be received more than once, whenever a person falls gravely ill again. 'Last Rites' more properly refers to the final sacraments given to the dying, which include this Anointing along with Confession and Viaticum (final Communion), but the Anointing itself is for anyone seriously sick, meant to heal and console, not only to prepare for death.

en.answer_full:
> "Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven." — James 5:14–15

The **Anointing of the Sick** is among the most misunderstood sacraments in Catholic life. It is widely reduced in popular imagination to "Last Rites" — a final spiritual formality administered at the moment of death — when in fact it is a rich sacrament of healing, comfort, and grace available to any member of the faithful who faces serious illness, debilitating age, or significant surgery. Understanding it correctly requires both careful biblical exegesis and attention to the full scope of the Church's sacramental theology.

---

## What the Sacrament Actually Is

The Anointing of the Sick is one of the seven sacraments instituted by Christ for the healing of the whole person — body, soul, and spirit. It is administered by a priest (or bishop), who anoints the forehead and hands of the sick person with oil blessed by the bishop, while praying the words of the rite. The *Catechism of the Catholic Church* (n. 1511) teaches that it was instituted by Christ and commended to the faithful by the Apostle James. It is not a sacrament of death but a sacrament of the Church's pastoral care for those who suffer.

The name "Extreme Unction" — the older designation meaning "final anointing" — was never wrong in itself but became misleading when it led people to delay calling a priest until a person was unconscious or hours from death. The Second Vatican Council deliberately restored the earlier and more accurate name — **Anointing of the Sick** — to recover the sacrament's proper scope and encourage its timely reception.

---

## Exegetical Analysis: James 5:14–15

The primary scriptural foundation for this sacrament is James 5:14–15, and it deserves careful examination. The text reads: "Is anyone among you sick? Let him call for the elders [*presbyterous*] of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord. And the prayer of faith will save [*sōsei*] the one who is sick, and the Lord will raise him up. And if he has committed sins, he will be forgiven."

Several features of this text are theologically decisive. First, the agents are the *presbyteroi* — the elders of the Church, the same term used throughout the New Testament for ordained leaders. This is not an instruction for any believer to anoint any other believer; it is a structured ecclesial act. Second, the anointing is done "in the name of the Lord" — a phrase that in the New Testament consistently marks acts of sacramental authority. Third, the verb *sōsei* ("will save") carries the full Hellenistic biblical range of physical rescue, restoration to health, and eschatological salvation. The sentence does not say "may help" but "will save" — expressing the confident efficacy of the sacramental act. Fourth, the forgiveness of sins is connected directly to the anointing, not as a separate act but as part of the same sacramental event. This pairing of physical and spiritual healing is characteristic of how Jesus himself healed throughout the Gospels.

Some critics argue that James 5 describes a charismatic healing prayer, not a formal sacrament. But this misreads the text's institutional language. The *presbyteroi* are summoned, not just any Spirit-filled believer. The oil is applied in formal anointing, not merely in spontaneous prayer. The promise of forgiveness is attached to the act. All these features align with the Church's understanding of sacramental action.

---

## Biblical Evidence

### Mark 6:13 — The Apostolic Practice of Healing Anointing

"And they cast out many demons and anointed with oil many who were sick and healed them." The Twelve are already anointing the sick with oil during the ministry of Jesus himself, at his commission. This is not incidental; it establishes that healing anointing with oil was a recognized apostolic practice from the very beginning of the Church's mission, continuous with what James later codifies into ecclesial structure.

### Luke 10:34 — Oil as a Vehicle of Healing

The Good Samaritan "bound up his wounds, pouring on oil and wine." While this is not a sacramental text, it reflects the ancient Near Eastern understanding of oil as a healing agent — an understanding the early Church carried into its sacramental use.

### John 9:6–7 — Jesus's Physical Instrumentality in Healing

Jesus heals the man born blind by making clay and applying it to his eyes — a deliberate physical act accompanying a spiritual and miraculous healing. The pattern of physical instrumentality in healing is not accidental but reflects Christ's incarnational approach: spiritual grace conveyed through material means. This pattern underlies all sacramental theology, including the Anointing of the Sick.

---

## Core Theological Distinction: Therapeutic vs. Salvific Healing

The Anointing of the Sick addresses the **total condition** of the seriously ill person, not merely their physical symptoms. The *Catechism* (n. 1520) enumerates four distinct graces conferred by the sacrament:

The first grace is a special strengthening by the Holy Spirit — courage, peace, and fortitude against the temptations that accompany serious illness, including discouragement, despair, and the fear of death. The second is the union of the sick person's suffering with the Passion of Christ, so that their suffering becomes redemptive — offered as a participation in Christ's saving work. The third is an ecclesial grace: the sick person is not alone but supported by the intercession of the whole Church. The fourth is preparation for the final passage when the sacrament is received near death — what is legitimately called "Last Rites" when combined with Viaticum (final reception of Holy Communion) and final absolution.

The key distinction is between **healing as cure** and **healing as restoration of the whole person to God's purposes**. The sacrament does not guarantee physical recovery — though it may accompany it — but it always confers spiritual healing, strengthening, and alignment with the will of God. This is why the sick person who receives it may die, yet die in peace, forgiven, strengthened, and united to Christ's offering on the Cross.

---

## Patristic Witness

### Pope Innocent I (d. 417)

> "There is no doubt that this passage [James 5:14] is to be received or understood of the faithful who are sick, who can be anointed with the holy oil of chrism, which has been prepared by the bishop, and not only priests but all Christians may use it for anointing, when their own needs or those of their family demand." — *Epistle to Decentius*, 8

Innocent I's letter, written in response to a question about the practice of anointing, is the earliest papal document explicitly addressing the sacrament. It confirms both the ecclesial structure (oil blessed by the bishop) and the broad pastoral application to all the sick, not only the dying.

### Origen (c. 185–254)

> "There is a third type of forgiveness of sins, through penance... where he who is sick summons the elders of the Church and they pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord, and the prayer of faith will heal the sick man, and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him." — *Homilies on Leviticus*, 2.4

Origen's treatment shows that the Church in his time understood James 5:14–15 precisely as the New Testament basis for a practice of sacramental anointing and forgiveness — not merely a charismatic healing prayer.

### Caesarius of Arles (c. 470–542)

> "As often as some infirmity overtakes a man, let him who is ill receive the Body and Blood of Christ, and then let him anoint his body with the blessed oil... For thus, according to what the Apostle James says, not only shall his body be healed but also his soul." — *Sermon*, 19.5

Caesarius exhorts his congregation to receive the Anointing of the Sick promptly when illness strikes — not to wait until death — and connects it explicitly to James 5 and to the healing of both body and soul.

---

## Ecumenical Council Definition

The **Council of Trent** (Session XIV, Chapter 1, 1551) defined: "This sacred anointing of the sick was instituted as a true and proper sacrament of the New Testament by Christ our Lord, hinted at indeed in Mark (6:13) but commended to the faithful and promulgated by James the Apostle... This sacrament confers grace, remits sins, and comforts the sick." Trent explicitly rejected the idea that this is merely a human religious custom, defining it as a sacrament of divine institution with real efficacy.

---

## CCC Reference Table

| Reference | Teaching |
|---|---|
| CCC 1499 | The Anointing of the Sick is a sacrament of healing for the seriously ill |
| CCC 1511 | The sacrament was instituted by Christ and entrusted to the Church |
| CCC 1514 | The proper recipients are the faithful who are seriously ill or elderly |
| CCC 1520 | The sacrament confers strength, forgiveness, union with Christ, and preparation for death |
| CCC 1521 | The sick person's suffering is united to Christ's Passion for the good of the Church |
| CCC 1532 | The sacrament is a preparation for the final journey and completion of penance |

---

## Common Objections

**"Catholics only call the priest when someone is dying — isn't this a death ritual?"** The association with dying is a historical accident, not the Church's teaching. The sacrament is properly for anyone seriously ill, facing surgery, or weakened by age. The Church actively encourages Catholics not to wait until someone is unconscious or hours from death, as the full spiritual benefits require the person's conscious participation when possible.

**"James 5 is about charismatic healing prayer, not a formal sacrament."** The text's own language — *presbyteroi* (ordained elders), anointing "in the name of the Lord," connected forgiveness of sins — signals institutional ecclesial action, not spontaneous charismatic prayer. Every element of the verse aligns with the Church's understanding of sacramental form.

**"Oil doesn't have any supernatural power — this is superstition."** The oil itself has no inherent power; it is a vehicle of the Spirit's action, as water is in Baptism. The grace comes from Christ acting through the Church's prayer and the sacramental sign, not from any chemical property of olive oil. This is basic Catholic sacramental theology: grace is conveyed through material signs because Christ himself is the Word made flesh.

---

## Conclusion

The Anointing of the Sick is a sacrament of profound pastoral mercy — one that the Church has administered continuously since the apostolic era, grounded in the explicit text of James 5 and in the healing ministry of Jesus himself. Reclaiming its proper name and proper recipients from the shadow of "Last Rites" is not a modern liberal revision but a recovery of the sacrament's original, Gospel-rooted meaning: that Christ, through his Church, accompanies the sick, heals the whole person, and ensures that no one faces suffering or death alone.

objections.response: James gives an explicit instruction: "Is anyone among you sick? He should summon the presbyters (elders/priests) of the church, and they should pray over him and anoint him with oil in the name of the Lord, and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up. If he has committed any sins, he will be forgiven" (James 5:14-15). This describes exactly what the Church calls the Anointing of the Sick: a summoned priest, prayer, oil, and both physical and spiritual healing.
objections.objection: Praying for physical healing is fine, but anointing the sick with oil as a formal sacrament administered by a priest has no clear New Testament command.

objections.response: James's instruction can't be reduced to ordinary medicine — he explicitly ties the anointing to prayer "in the name of the Lord," to faith, and to forgiveness of sins (James 5:15), effects no medicinal oil produces on its own. That combination — a summoned elder of the Church, prayer of faith, and forgiveness of sins tied to physical anointing — is precisely what marks it as a sacred rite, not a home remedy.
objections.objection: This anointing was just a common first-century medical practice — oil was used as medicine in the ancient world, not a sacramental rite (compare the Good Samaritan pouring "oil and wine" on the man's wounds, Luke 10:34).
